## 1. Purpose

This SOP describes procedures for collecting, handling, and preserving
plant tissue samples in the field for subsequent laboratory analysis.
Plant tissue analysis provides data on nutrient concentrations (C, N,
P, K, metals), stable isotope ratios ($\delta^{13}$C, $\delta^{15}$N),
and other biogeochemical parameters [@kalra1998; @mills2004]. Proper
sampling technique is essential to ensure that results represent the
target tissue and are not contaminated or degraded during collection
and transport.

Foliar nutrient concentrations and leaf mass per area (LMA) form part
of the "leaf economics spectrum," a global axis of plant strategy that
links leaf structure to function across biomes [@wright2004].
Standardized sampling protocols allow EA Program data to be compared
with global trait databases and regional reference values
[@cornelissen2003].


## 2. Scope

- **Applies to:** Collection of leaf, stem, root, and reproductive
  tissue from vascular plants for nutrient and isotope analysis at all
  EA Program field sites
- **Does not apply to:** Soil organic matter sampling (see
  [SOP-F400](SOP-F400-soil-sampling.qmd)); algal tissue sampling;
  plant tissue culture; DNA extraction from plant tissue (see
  [SOP-L700](../lab_sops/SOP-L700-dna-extraction.qmd))
- **Location:** All EA Program field sites; initial processing in
  SGM 133/134


## 3. Responsibilities

| Role              | Responsibility                              |
|:------------------|:--------------------------------------------|
| PI / Field Lead   | Approve sampling design and target species  |
| Trained Personnel | Collect and process tissue per this SOP     |
| New Students      | Complete training before independent sampling |


## 4. Safety and Hazards

::: {.callout-warning}
### Hazards

- **Biological:** Contact with allergenic plants (poison oak, stinging
  nettles). Some target species may have thorns or irritating sap.
- **Physical:** Use of pruning shears and scissors poses a laceration
  risk.
- **Chemical:** If using liquid nitrogen for snap-freezing, follow
  cryogenic safety procedures (gloves, face shield, ventilated area).
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Nitrile gloves
- [ ] Closed-toe shoes or field boots
- [ ] Sun protection
- [ ] Leather gloves (for thorny species)
- [ ] Cryogenic gloves and face shield (if using liquid nitrogen)

### Emergency Procedures

For cuts from pruning shears, apply direct pressure and clean the
wound. For poison oak exposure, wash with cold water and soap as soon
as possible. Refer to
[SOP-F001 Field Safety](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd).


## 5. Definitions

- **Tissue type:** The specific plant organ sampled (e.g., fully
  expanded mature leaves, current-year stem growth, fine roots less
  than 2 mm diameter, seeds).
- **Composite sample:** A sample formed by combining tissue from
  multiple individuals of the same species within a plot to represent
  the population average.
- **Voucher specimen:** A pressed and identified plant specimen
  collected alongside tissue samples to verify species identification.
- **Leaf mass per area (LMA):** The ratio of leaf dry mass to
  one-sided leaf area (g m^-2^); a key functional trait inversely
  related to specific leaf area (SLA) [@wright2004].


## 6. Required Materials

| Item                                     | Notes                              |
|:-----------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------|
| Stainless steel pruning shears or scissors | Clean between species             |
| Paper coin envelopes or labeled paper bags | For drying samples; avoid plastic for fresh tissue intended for drying |
| Ziplock bags (gallon size)               | For fresh tissue requiring freezing |
| Cooler with ice packs                    | For transport of fresh tissue      |
| Permanent markers (Sharpie)              | For labeling                       |
| Pre-printed labels                       | Site, species, tissue type, date, collector |
| DI water squeeze bottle                  | For rinsing contamination          |
| Ethanol (70%) in a spray bottle          | For decontaminating tools between species |
| Paper towels                             | For drying tools after decontamination |
| GPS unit                                 | For recording sampling locations   |
| Plant identification guides              | For species verification           |
| Plant press (if collecting vouchers)     | See [SOP-F603](SOP-F603-vegetation-transect-surveys.qmd) Section 9 |
| Field data sheet                         | Pre-printed                        |
| Liquid nitrogen dewar and cryo-vials     | Only if snap-freezing is required  |
| Analytical balance (field-portable, optional) | For recording fresh mass        |


## 7. Estimated Time

| Task                                   | Time                         |
|:---------------------------------------|:-----------------------------|
| Site setup and species identification  | 15--30 minutes               |
| Tissue collection (10 samples)         | 30--60 minutes               |
| Labeling and packing for transport     | 15 minutes                   |
| Lab processing (cleaning, drying)      | Variable (see Section 9)     |


## 8. Procedure

### 8.1 Sampling Design

1. Define the target species, tissue type, and number of replicates
   in the sampling plan before going to the field
2. Determine whether individual or composite samples are needed. For
   nutrient analysis where individual variation is important, collect
   tissue from individual plants. For site-level averages, composite
   tissue from 5--10 individuals per species per plot.
3. Select individuals randomly within the sampling area. Avoid plants
   at plot edges, obviously damaged or diseased individuals, and
   plants with heavy herbivory or epiphyte loads (unless these are the
   target condition).

### 8.2 Leaf Tissue Collection

1. Put on clean nitrile gloves. Change gloves between species to
   avoid cross-contamination.
2. Select fully expanded, mature leaves from the upper canopy (sun
   leaves) unless the project specifically targets shade leaves or
   another position. Standardizing canopy position is critical for
   comparability; sun and shade leaves can differ by 20--40% in leaf
   nitrogen concentration and LMA [@cornelissen2003].
3. Using clean pruning shears, clip the petiole at its base. For
   grasses, clip the most recent fully expanded blade at the ligule.
4. Collect enough tissue mass for the planned analyses. As a guideline:

| Analysis                          | Minimum dry mass   |
|:----------------------------------|:-------------------|
| C, N, S by EA-IRMS               | 2--5 mg            |
| $\delta^{13}$C, $\delta^{15}$N   | 2--5 mg            |
| Total P, metals (acid digestion)  | 100--500 mg        |
| Multiple analyses from one sample | 2--5 g fresh weight recommended |

5. For composite samples, collect an approximately equal mass of
   tissue from each individual and combine in a single bag.
6. Place tissue immediately into a labeled paper envelope (if
   air-drying) or a labeled Ziplock bag (if freezing or transporting
   fresh). For frozen samples, place bags into the cooler with ice
   packs.

### 8.3 Stem, Root, and Reproductive Tissue

- **Stems:** Clip current-year growth. Record the diameter and length
  of the stem segment.
- **Fine roots (less than 2 mm diameter):** Excavate carefully around
  the base of the target plant using a trowel. Separate live roots
  from dead roots and soil. Rinse briefly with DI water in the field
  or at the first opportunity in the lab.
- **Seeds/fruits:** Collect from a minimum of 5 individuals. Record
  the phenological stage (e.g., immature, mature, dehisced).

### 8.4 Decontamination Between Species

1. Spray pruning shears with 70% ethanol
2. Wipe dry with a clean paper towel
3. Allow to air-dry for 30 seconds before cutting the next species
4. For metal analysis, use stainless steel tools only (no galvanized
   or painted tools) and rinse with DI water after ethanol to remove
   residual salts

### 8.5 Labeling

Every sample must be labeled with:

- Site name and plot/transect ID
- Species (use the 6-letter code from
  [SOP-F603](SOP-F603-vegetation-transect-surveys.qmd) Section 11.2)
- Tissue type (leaf, stem, root, seed)
- Individual or composite (if composite, record the number of
  individuals)
- Date (YYYY-MM-DD)
- Collector initials

Write on both the bag/envelope and a separate tag inside (in case
the exterior label smudges).

### 8.6 Field Data Sheet

Record the following for each sample:

| Field                | Entry                               |
|:---------------------|:------------------------------------|
| Sample ID            | Unique sequential number            |
| Site / Plot          |                                     |
| Species              |                                     |
| Tissue type          |                                     |
| Number of individuals| (if composite)                      |
| GPS coordinates      |                                     |
| Fresh mass (g)       | (if field balance available)        |
| Notes                | Condition, herbivory, phenology     |


## 9. Sample Preservation and Lab Processing

### 9.1 Drying

The default preservation method for nutrient and isotope analysis
[@jones2001]:

1. Transport paper envelopes to the lab within 24 hours
2. Dry at 60 C in the drying oven
   ([SOP-L105](../lab_sops/SOP-L105-drying-ovens.qmd)) for at least
   48 hours or until a constant mass is reached
3. Record the dry mass
4. Store dried tissue in labeled coin envelopes in a desiccator or
   sealed container until grinding

::: {.callout-important}
### Temperature Matters
Do not exceed 60 C for tissue intended for nitrogen or carbon isotope
analysis. Higher temperatures can volatilize nitrogen compounds and
alter $\delta^{15}$N values [@kalra1998].
:::

### 9.2 Freezing

For analyses requiring fresh tissue (enzyme assays, gene expression,
volatile compounds):

1. Transport in cooler with ice packs (or snap-freeze with liquid
   nitrogen in the field)
2. Transfer to the -80 C freezer
   ([SOP-L106](../lab_sops/SOP-L106-refrigerators-freezers.qmd))
   within 6 hours of collection
3. Record in the freezer inventory

### 9.3 Grinding

1. Grind dried tissue to a fine powder using a ball mill or mortar
   and pestle
2. Clean the grinding equipment between samples (brush, then wipe
   with ethanol)
3. Store ground tissue in labeled microcentrifuge tubes or coin
   envelopes


## 10. Quality Control

- Collect at least one field blank per sampling event: open an empty
  labeled bag at the site, expose it to the same conditions as the
  samples, then seal and process identically
- For metal analysis, verify that tools are stainless steel and
  DI-rinsed
- Record the time between collection and drying/freezing on the data
  sheet; flag any samples exceeding the 24-hour (drying) or 6-hour
  (freezing) window
- For composite samples, verify that approximately equal mass was
  contributed by each individual
- When interpreting foliar nutrient results, compare against published
  reference ranges for the target species or functional group
  [@reuter1997; @mills2004]

## 12. Training Record

Before collecting plant tissue independently, personnel must:

1. Read this SOP and [SOP-F001 Field Safety](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd)
2. Demonstrate species identification for the target community
3. Demonstrate proper collection technique (glove changes, tool
   decontamination, labeling)
4. Process one set of samples through drying and grinding under
   supervision
5. Be signed off by the PI or field lead
